findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend AC1 to require a server restart (or proof that config is read per request) and evidence from a real production plan-review call showing the 5.5 model id in server logs or Bedrock invocation records.
evidence: "a fresh in-container resolution shows frontier/standard/trivial on the 5.5 ids"
Observed: "Live MCP container ... up ~23 h"
findings.finding: AC1's proof runs `LLMConfig.from_env()` in a fresh process inside the container. That does not show the long-running MCP server, which has been up about 23 hours, uses the 5.5 models. If config is loaded at server startup, the server still serves 4.x until restarted. No criterion requires a restart or a real plan review showing the 5.5 model id.
scenarios: The workspace is repaired and a fresh process resolves 5.5, but the server process still sends opus-4-8 to Bedrock.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add negative-case tests to AC2: the entrypoint still refuses (and surfaces) a dirty tree that does not exactly match a commit strictly between HEAD and origin/main, including uncommitted edits and untracked files.
evidence: "with a test reproducing the stuck state"
"clean against a descendant commit of HEAD that is an ancestor of origin/main"
findings.finding: AC2's test requirement only reproduces the stuck state (the positive case). 'Recovered safely' hinges on the boundary of the qualifying condition. The plan does not require tests showing that dirty trees outside that condition are still refused: trees matching no commit, real uncommitted edits, a commit not an ancestor of origin/main, or untracked files. The existing refusal behavior is being changed without corresponding preserve-guard test work.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria — AC2 ('with a test reproducing the stuck state')
scenarios: The recovery predicate is too loose (e.g. it only checks that the index equals some commit tree), and an operator's in-progress hotfix in the workspace is reset away while the positive-case test stays green.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the quoted log line in Observed to the emitted text `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing to refresh` (and optionally mention the new `MCP_CODE_WORKSPACE_ERROR {"reason": "dirty"…}` marker).
evidence: Plan: "logs `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing refresh`"
infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh:268: echo "mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing to refresh" >&2
Later ticket comment quotes it correctly: "logged `dirty code checkout — refusing to refresh`"
findings.finding: The plan quotes the refusal log line as `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing refresh`. The entrypoint actually emits `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing to refresh`. An exact-string journal search using the plan's quote would find nothing.
findings.location: ## Observed, bullet 5 ("every restart since logs `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing refresh`")
scenarios: An operator copies the plan's string into journalctl -g to confirm or count past refusals and gets zero hits, wrongly concluding the refusal never happened.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing refresh` with `mcp: dirty code checkout — refusing to refresh`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Pick one AC2 design (recover-then-alert, or alert-only), name the concrete surfacing mechanism (e.g. container healthcheck goes unhealthy plus a named alarm), and add an Approach section describing the entrypoint change.
evidence: "is either recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health)"
The plan has no Approach/Plan section; the only sections are Observed, Hypotheses, Impact and Acceptance criteria.
findings.finding: AC2 leaves the core design decision to the executor. The fix may either auto-recover the stuck state or alarm on it, and 'alarm/health' does not name a mechanism (health-check failure, CloudWatch metric, log-based alarm). No approach section anywhere in the plan resolves this.
scenarios: One executor ships only a log line it calls 'loud', while another builds auto-recovery with no alerting; both claim AC2.
findings.suggested_fix: Recommend both: under the refresh lock, if the tree is clean against a commit C where HEAD is an ancestor of C and C is an ancestor of origin/main, run `git update-ref HEAD C` (keeping the index and tree as they are) and then continue the normal fast-forward. For any other dirty state, mark the container healthcheck unhealthy and emit a metric or alarm, not just stderr.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] For AC2, cite the PR/commit and the exact test command (e.g. `pytest tests/...::test_interrupted_ff_recovery`); for AC3, link the ticket comment listing every source searched (rebar-mcp journal, autodeploy logs, dmesg/OOM, docker events, SSM history) with time windows. Otherwise uncheck both boxes.
evidence: "- [x] The interrupted-fast-forward state ... with a test reproducing the stuck state." — no test path or command
"- [x] Root cause of the interruption identified or the evidence searched recorded."
Hypotheses: "The killer is unidentified"
findings.finding: AC2 and AC3 are checked [x] with no evidence. There is no PR/commit, no test name or command, and no location where the root-cause search is recorded. The Hypotheses section says the cause is still unidentified.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria AC2, AC3 vs Hypotheses section
scenarios: A reviewer cannot tell whether the entrypoint fix and its test actually exist, or where the search record lives.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record in AC1 the origin/main SHA the '0 0' was computed against, after a fresh `git fetch`, and state whether parity with GitHub main is required.
evidence: "Its `origin/main` was fetched to `06b3b1a5230`; GitHub main is now `91182f96362`."
"reports `0 0` against origin/main"
findings.finding: The '0 0 against origin/main' check depends on unstated prior state. The workspace's origin/main was 06b3b1a5230 while GitHub main is 91182f96362. Without a fetch first, '0 0' shows parity with a stale remote-tracking ref, not with GitHub main.
scenarios: The recorded '0 0' was computed against 06b3b1a5230 and is described as 'fresh' even though it is behind GitHub main.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the output of `git fetch origin && git rev-parse HEAD origin/main && git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...origin/main` in the ticket comment.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a criterion that workspace writes (refresh and recovery) run under the single refresh lock, are idempotent if re-run after a kill at any point (a test kills mid-update), and are not interrupted by the autodeploy reconcile, e.g. reconcile skips restart while the lock is held.
evidence: "autodeploy ran its 2-minute MCP reconcile throughout"
"a fast-forward ... that wrote index and working tree but never moved HEAD (process killed between the two)"
No AC covers atomicity or concurrency of workspace writes.
findings.finding: Nothing addresses recurrence. The fix only detects or recovers the post-crash state; it does not make the fast-forward resistant to interruption. Autodeploy's 2-minute reconcile ran throughout the window and is a plausible killer. The plan also does not require auto-recovery to run under the same lock as refresh_code_locked or with the autodeploy loop excluded.
scenarios: Autodeploy restarts the container mid-recovery, leaving yet another partial state.
The recovery and a concurrent refresh race on the same workspace (check-then-act).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Require that any refresh refusal, not only the interrupted-fast-forward shape, is surfaced through the same alarm/health mechanism.
evidence: "The refusal is stderr-only; nothing alerted."
AC2 scopes to "The interrupted-fast-forward state (clean against a descendant commit of HEAD ...)"
findings.finding: The general dirty-tree refusal stays stderr-only for every state other than the specific interrupted-fast-forward shape. If the entrypoint auto-recovers that one shape, any other dirty state would still go silently stale, which is how this incident went unnoticed.
scenarios: A genuinely modified file in the workspace blocks refresh for weeks with no alert.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record the exact git commands SSM 86220c94 ran, why they were non-destructive given the index matched e2ed08b343a, and the pre-repair SHA/state saved for back-out.
evidence: "repair by SSM command 86220c94" — the operation itself is unspecified
findings.finding: The production repair (SSM command 86220c94) is a write to the shared production workspace, but the plan never describes the operation (e.g. `update-ref HEAD e2ed08b343a` and then ff-only, vs `reset --hard`). It also records no back-out (the pre-repair HEAD and index state to restore if needed).
scenarios: A `reset --hard` would discard state that a different hypothesis would need for root-cause analysis.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC to update review-bot-ops.md "MCP code workspace freshness" with the interrupted-fast-forward signature, the entrypoint's recovery or alarm behavior, and the manual repair steps.
evidence: "(runbook review-bot-ops.md \"MCP code workspace freshness\")" is cited, but there is no AC to update it
findings.finding: The plan introduces a new failure signature and either a new recovery behavior or a new alarm, but does not require updating the runbook section it cites. Operators would then lack guidance on what the alarm means and how to respond.
scenarios: The new alarm fires and the on-call operator has no runbook step for it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In AC2, state the disposition per arm: what the health check and serving do when the stuck state is detected (degraded-and-serving vs fatal), and what surfaces when auto-recovery itself fails. Recovery failure must still be surfaced loudly, never fall back to a stderr-only refusal.
evidence: "is either recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health)"
"The entrypoint's `refresh_code_locked` refuses a dirty tree ... The refusal is stderr-only; nothing alerted."
There is no statement of whether the health check fails, or whether serving continues on stale code, under each arm.
findings.finding: AC2 alters how the entrypoint handles a degraded (dirty/stale) workspace but states no disposition per arm. It leaves 'recovered safely' vs 'surfaced loudly' undecided. It does not say whether a surfaced stuck state is fatal (container reports unhealthy, may restart-loop and take MCP down) or non-fatal (keeps serving stale config while the alarm fires). It also does not say what surfaces when the recovery attempt itself fails, for example a git reset error or a tree that matches no qualifying commit.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria — AC2 ('either recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health)')
scenarios: The implementer wires a failing health check, autodeploy's 2-minute reconcile restarts the container repeatedly, and plan review becomes unavailable instead of merely stale.
Recovery is chosen, the reset fails partway, and the entrypoint falls back to the old silent stderr refusal, so the original 13-day silent staleness recurs.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' line such as: 'Stuck/dirty workspace → keep serving the current checkout (non-fatal), emit an alarm-visible health/degraded signal naming HEAD vs origin/main. Auto-recovery failure → same loud degraded signal; never silently refuse.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend AC2 so that every refresh refusal (and workspace HEAD lagging origin/main beyond the reconcile window) is surfaced via alarm/health, not only the interrupted-fast-forward shape, even when that shape is auto-recovered.
evidence: "The refusal is stderr-only; nothing alerted."
"The interrupted-fast-forward state (clean against a descendant commit of HEAD that is an ancestor of origin/main) is either recovered safely ... or surfaced loudly"
findings.finding: The observed defect is general: any dirty-tree refusal (and any HEAD-behind-origin/main staleness) is stderr-only and went unalerted for about 13 days. AC2 only requires handling the single interrupted-fast-forward shape, and it may be satisfied by recovery alone. Other dirty or stale states would then remain silent, so the plan delivers less than the problem it demonstrates.
findings.location: Observed (last bullet) vs Acceptance criteria — AC2
scenarios: A genuine local edit in the workspace (or a fetch that stops advancing origin/main) leaves production on old models indefinitely with no alarm. The recovery-only path satisfies AC2 but does not catch this.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Update the Hypotheses section to state the identified root cause (an OOM kill of rebar-mcp-e2ed08b343a2-8092 at 2026-10-28 17:47:26 PDT, mid `git merge --ff-only`) and cite the kernel cgroup-OOM journal line, so AC3 rests on text in the plan.
evidence: Plan: "The killer is unidentified: the rebar-mcp journal has no entries in that window"
infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh:239-241: "A fast-forward killed between writing the tree and moving HEAD (observed: the container was OOM-killed mid-refresh)"
infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md:83: "(observed when the container was OOM-killed mid-refresh)"
tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py:478: "reddish-drinkable-canvasback: the container was OOM-killed mid-refresh"
Ticket comment (root cause): kernel 'Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 1648385 (rebar-mcp)' at 2026-10-29 00:47:26 UTC; index mtime 00:47:28
findings.finding: The Hypotheses section still says the killer is unidentified. The repo and the ticket record now say the container was OOM-killed mid-refresh. So the plan text contradicts the implementation it is supposed to describe, and AC3 is checked against reasoning the plan body does not contain.
findings.location: ## Hypotheses (unproven) / AC3 'Root cause of the interruption identified or the evidence searched recorded'
scenarios: A reviewer or verifier reads only the plan body and concludes AC3 was satisfied through the 'evidence searched recorded' branch, when the root cause was actually identified.
Someone later trusts the plan's 'unidentified' hypothesis and reopens the investigation, or misses the link to OOM/memory-limit work.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename the section to 'Root cause' and replace 'The killer is unidentified…' with: 'Kernel journal 2026-10-29 00:47:26 UTC: Memory cgroup out of memory killed rebar-mcp (container rebar-mcp-e2ed08b343a2-8092, cgroup limit 3801088 kB, RSS ~3.37 GB minutes before); the index mtime 00:47:28 matches the interrupted refresh_code_locked fast-forward.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an edit-set to the plan naming infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh (recover_interrupted_fast_forward, refresh_code_locked), infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh (MCP_CODE_PROBE, mcp_check_code_workspace), infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md 'MCP code workspace freshness', tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py and tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_mcp_bluegreen.py.
evidence: The plan names only `refresh_code_locked` and cites 'runbook review-bot-ops.md "MCP code workspace freshness"' as the place to read the `0 0` check, not as a file to change.
infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md:77-90 had to be rewritten: the entrypoint used to simply refuse a dirty tree, and the section now describes the recovery and the mcp-code-workspace-stuck page.
infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:698-725 (MCP_CODE_PROBE / mcp_check_code_workspace) is the 'surfaced loudly' half and lives outside the entrypoint.
The tests sit in two directories: tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py:484-560 and tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_mcp_bluegreen.py:2837.
findings.finding: The plan never lists which files the fix touches. AC2 can only be met by editing files outside the entrypoint: the autodeploy tick check, the deploy_errors alarm path, the runbook paragraph that described the old refuse-dirty behaviour, and two test files in different directories. None of these are named, so a reviewer cannot tell which files are in scope from the plan alone.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria — AC2 ('recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health), with a test reproducing the stuck state'); there is no edit-set / file-impact section
scenarios: A reviewer checks that the fix is fully done and misses that the runbook text still described the old 'refuse dirty' contract.

A later change to the entrypoint's recovery rule updates mcp-entrypoint.sh but not the separate autodeploy probe, which also decides what counts as 'dirty'/'behind' (MCP_CODE_PROBE), so the two disagree.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Files touched' section listing: infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh (new recover_interrupted_fast_forward, called from refresh_code_locked); infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh (MCP_CODE_PROBE + mcp_check_code_workspace emitting AUTODEPLOY_ERROR mcp-code-workspace-stuck, which pages through the existing rebar-autodeploy-errors alarm); infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md 'MCP code workspace freshness' (document the recovery and the page); tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py (stuck-state reproduction plus the untracked/unstaged/unreachable negative cases); tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_mcp_bluegreen.py (stuck-workspace marker).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Change AC2 from 'either recover or surface' to 'both': recover the provable interrupted-fast-forward state, AND alarm (page) on any workspace that stays dirty, diverged, unreachable, or behind the live image commit.
evidence: Plan Observed: "The refusal is stderr-only; nothing alerted."
Plan AC2: "is either recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health)"
Hypotheses: "The killer is unidentified", so the interruption can recur at a different point in the fast-forward and leave a state the recovery predicate rejects
findings.finding: AC2 lets the implementer pick either entrypoint recovery or loud surfacing. The named failure was that a stuck workspace sat unalerted for about 13 days. Recovering only the exact 'index == later origin/main commit' state does not fix that for any other interrupted-refresh state, such as a kill partway through writing the tree, where the working tree differs from the index or the index matches no ancestry-path commit. Those states would still be refused with output only on stderr.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria, AC2 ("either recovered safely by the entrypoint or surfaced loudly (alarm/health)")
scenarios: The refresh is killed after the index is written but while the working tree is half-written: recover_interrupted_fast_forward bails at `git diff --quiet`. Under the 'recover' branch of the AC, no alarm exists, so gates go stale silently again.
The refresh is killed during the index write: write-tree matches no ancestry-path commit, recovery returns 1, and only stderr gets the refusal.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite AC2 as: "The entrypoint recovers the provable interrupted-fast-forward state (clean against a descendant of HEAD that is an ancestor of origin/main) with a test that reproduces it; AND any workspace state the entrypoint still refuses (dirty/diverged/unreachable, or HEAD not containing the live image commit) pages through an existing alarm, with a test."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a short Approach paragraph that names the chosen mechanism (ref-only compare-and-swap recovery under the checkout lock, plus a per-tick alarm) and why it fits: no file is rewritten or discarded under a gate that may be reading the workspace.
evidence: ABSENCE: the plan has Observed / Hypotheses / Impact / Acceptance criteria sections only. No section names the chosen mechanism or why it suits this codebase.
AC2 is stated as a disjunction ("either ... or ..."), not as a decision.
findings.finding: The plan never says which remedy it chose or why it fits. It has no approach or rationale section: AC2 offers two alternatives and does not explain why the chosen one (ref-only compare-and-swap recovery under the existing checkout lock, plus a deploy-tick probe) fits the entrypoint's refuse-rather-than-reset design better than resetting or recloning the checkout.
findings.location: Plan body (no Approach/Fix section); Acceptance criteria AC2
scenarios: An implementer or later reader cannot tell whether a reset/reclone recovery (which would rewrite files under a gate that may be reading them) would be acceptable, because the plan never states the 'never rewrite or discard on-disk content' property that makes ref-only recovery the right choice.
